'''Patrick O'Reilly Brown''' (born 1954) is an American [[geneticist]] and businessman who is the founder of [[Impossible Foods]] Inc.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.cnbc.com/2015/05/12/impossible-foods-disruptor-50.html | title=Impossible Foods 2015 Disruptor 50| website=[[CNBC]]| date=2015-05-12}}</ref> and professor emeritus in the department of [[biochemistry]] at [[Stanford University]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://biox.stanford.edu/about/people/affiliated-faculty/patrick-o-brown-professor-biochemistry-emeritus | title=Patrick O. Brown - Professor of Biochemistry, Emeritus &#124; Welcome to Bio-X| date=12 March 2014}}</ref> Brown is co-founder of the [[Public Library of Science]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Gitschier|first=Jane|date=2009-07-17|title=You Say You Want a Revolution: An Interview with Pat Brown|journal=PLOS Genetics|language=en|volume=5|issue=7|article-number=e1000560|doi=10.1371/journal.pgen.1000560|issn=1553-7404|pmc=2705184|pmid=19609358 |doi-access=free }}</ref> inventor of the [[DNA microarray]],<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.dnalc.org/view/15036-Why-we-developed-the-microarray-Patrick-Brown.html | title=Why we developed the microarray, Patrick Brown :: DNA Learning Center}}</ref> and a former investigator at [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.hhmi.org/scientists/patrick-o-brown | title=Patrick O. Brown}}</ref>

==Education==
Brown received each of his degrees from the [[University of Chicago]], including his [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] in 1976 and [[Doctor of Medicine|M.D.]] in 1982. His [[Ph.D.]], granted in 1980 while under the guidance of [[Nicholas R. Cozzarelli]], involved the study of DNA [[topoisomerase]]s.<ref name=bmcb2013>{{Cite journal | last1 = Brown | first1 = P. O. | doi = 10.1186/1741-7007-11-33 | title = An interview with Patrick O Brown on the origins and future of open access | journal = BMC Biology | volume = 11 | pages = 33–110 | year = 2013 | pmid =  23587113| pmc =3626920 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Academic career==
After getting his medical degree in 1982, Brown completed a 3-year pediatric residency at [[Lurie Children's Hospital|Children's Memorial Hospital]] in Chicago but decided he could have a greater impact through basic research.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://www.dnalc.org/view/16013-Patrick-Henry-Brown|title=DNA Learning Center|access-date=2017-09-20|archive-date=2017-09-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170921045806/https://www.dnalc.org/view/16013-Patrick-Henry-Brown}}</ref> In 1985, Brown took a 3-year postdoctoral fellowship at the [[University of California]], San Francisco with [[J. Michael Bishop]] and [[Harold Varmus]] (who shared the 1989 Nobel Prize in Medicine for their discoveries about how genes can ignite cancerous tumors).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1989/summary/|title=The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1989|website=NobelPrize.org}}</ref> At UCSF, Brown and colleagues defined the mechanism by which [[retrovirus]]es, such as the [[HIV|HIV virus]], integrate their [[genes]] into the [[genome]] of the [[Cell (biology)|cell]]s they infect, which helped lead to development of new drugs to fight the disease.<ref name="Medicine of the Midway">{{cite web|title=Medicine of the Midway|url=http://www.uchospitals.edu/pdf/uch_008490.pdf/|date=Spring 2005}}</ref>

In 1988, Brown became an investigator of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and an assistant professor in the department of biochemistry at Stanford University School of Medicine, where he continued to investigate retroviral replication.<ref name="auto"/> In the early 1990s, Brown began developing a new technology to enable systematic investigation of the behavior and properties of whole genomes—called [[DNA microarrays]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Stanford Medicine Magazine|url=https://sm.stanford.edu/archive/stanmed/2005fall/microarray.html|date=Fall 2005}}</ref> "I had a mental image of a DNA microarray, even including the red and green fluorescent spots, a few years before I'd figured out the details of making them," Brown told The Scientist.<ref>{{cite web|title=The DNA Microarray|url=http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/16657/title/The-DNA-Microarray/|date=August 2005}}</ref>

Brown and his colleagues created a robotic dispenser that could deposit minute quantities of tens of thousands of individual genes onto a single [[Microscope slide|glass slide]], a "DNA microarray" or "gene chip." By flooding the slide with [[Fluorescence|fluorescently]] labeled genetic material derived from a living sample, a researcher could see which genes were being expressed in cells.<ref name="motherjones.com">{{Cite journal|title=Steal This Research Paper! (You Already Paid for It.)|url=https://www.motherjones.com/media/2013/09/michael-eisen-plos-open-access-aaron-swartz/|journal=Mother Jones|date=September 2013}}</ref> Shortly after their first description of DNA microarrays, the Brown laboratory published a "how-to" manual on the [[World Wide Web|Web]] that helped these robotic devices become standard equipment in life science labs throughout the world, in an effort led by [[Joseph DeRisi|Joe DeRisi]], [[Michael Eisen]], [[Ash Alizadeh]], and others.<ref name="Medicine of the Midway"/>

Brown and his colleagues developed experimental methods for using DNA microarrays to investigate basic principles of genome organization, gene expression, cell regulation and specialization, physiology, development and disease, and the [[microbiome]], along with statistical and computational tools for visualizing and interpreting the resulting large volumes of data. This work was especially revealing for the molecular portraits of many human cancers including lymphomas such as [[Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma|DLBCL]], [[Breast cancer classification|breast cancers]], and other tumors, as part of diverse global collaborations including [[David Botstein]], [[Michael Eisen]], [[Louis Staudt|Lou Staudt]], [[Ash Alizadeh]], and others. Microarray technologies are widely used for comparing gene expression patterns and other genome features among individuals and their tissues and cells, providing information on disease subcategories, disease prognosis, and treatment outcome.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=DNA microarrays: a powerful genomic tool for biomedical and clinical research|journal=Molecular Medicine|volume=13|issue=9–10|pages=527–541|pmc=1933257|date=2007-06-11|last1=Trevino|first1=V.|last2=Falciani|first2=F.|last3=Barrera-Saldaña|first3=H. A.|pmid=17660860|doi=10.2119/2006-00107.Trevino}}</ref>

Starting in the late 1990s, Brown began publicly voicing concern over what he called "a fundamentally flawed process of [[Academic publishing|scientific publishing]],"<ref name="Medicine of the Midway"/> in which academics typically published results of publicly funded research in private, commercial publishing houses that charged subscription fees for access to journals. "We viewed this entire process as being patently unfair. Not only were scientists in poor countries being denied access to the latest and best information out there, but the public who supports this research was being denied access as well. We felt there simply had to be a better way to do it," Brown told a University of Chicago medical journal.<ref name="Medicine of the Midway"/>

Brown began a collaboration with other scientists, including Harold Varmus (then director of the [[National Institutes of Health]]), [[David J. Lipman]] (then director of the [[National Center for Biotechnology Information]]), and [[Michael Eisen]] of [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]], to overhaul the scientific and medical publishing systems to make papers available on the rapidly developing Internet platforms such as [[Usenet]] and the World Wide Web.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=New Communication Paradigm for Science in the 21st Century|url=http://www.jyi.org/issue/new-communication-paradigm-for-science-in-the-21st-century/|journal=Journal of Young Investigators|date=May 2010|access-date=2017-09-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170921095011/http://www.jyi.org/issue/new-communication-paradigm-for-science-in-the-21st-century/|archive-date=2017-09-21}}</ref> "Why should publishers be able to control what I can do with information that was published by my scientific colleagues whose motivation was exactly to have their discoveries contribute to future discoveries? ... We had already existing tools that we could use to so to speak [[hyperlink]] things so that you could reorganize information in systematic ways, but they weren't really being exploited by the conventional scientific literature," Brown said in an interview with BioMedCentral Biology.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=An interview with Patrick O Brown on the origins and future of open access|pmc=3626920|journal= BMC Biology|volume=11|page=33|date=2013-04-15|last1=Brown|first1=P. O.|pmid=23587113|doi=10.1186/1741-7007-11-33 |doi-access=free }}</ref> The [[Nature (journal)|magazine Nature]] reported that the scientists' [[open-access]] movement could "spell the end for many print titles";<ref>{{Cite journal|title=The writing is on the web for science journals in print|journal=Nature|url=https://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v397/n6716/full/397195a0.html|date=1999-01-21|bibcode=1999Natur.397..195B|last1=Butler|first1=Declan|volume=397|issue=6716|pages=195–200|doi=10.1038/16544|pmid=9930685|s2cid=204990627|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Brown called subscription-based scientific journals "anachronisms."<ref name="motherjones.com"/>

In 2001, Brown, Eisen and Varmus co-founded the [[PLOS|Public Library of Science]] (PLOS) to make published scientific research open access and freely available to researchers in the scientific community.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Brower|first=Vicki|date=2001-11-15|title=Public library of science shifts gears|journal=EMBO Reports|volume=2|issue=11|pages=972–973|doi=10.1093/embo-reports/kve239|issn=1469-221X|pmc=1084138|pmid=11713184}}</ref> Funded by a grant from the [[Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation]], the [[non-profit organization]] advocated for designing alternative systems to fund for scientific publishing.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Eisen|first1=Michael B.|last2=Brown|first2=Patrick O.|last3=Varmus|first3=Harold E.|date=2002-09-12|title=Public-access group supports PubMed Central|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=419|issue=6903|page=111|doi=10.1038/419111c|issn=0028-0836|pmid=12226637|bibcode=2002Natur.419..111E|url=https://zenodo.org/record/1233223|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In 2002, Brown was elected to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]], identifying him as one of the top 2000 scientists in the nation. He is a member of the [[National Academy of Medicine]] and a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].<ref name="HHMI Bio">{{cite web|title=HHMI Bio|url=http://www.hhmi.org/research/investigators/brown_bio.html|publisher=HHMI|access-date=7 January 2013|archive-date=25 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120225120828/http://www.hhmi.org/research/investigators/brown_bio.html}}</ref>

==Impossible Foods==
In 2009, Brown took an 18-month [[sabbatical]] where he considered how to spend the rest of his career.<ref name="psmag.com">{{cite web|title=The Biography of a Plant-Based Burger: One man's mission to make meat obsolete|url=https://psmag.com/the-biography-of-a-plant-based-burger-31acbecb0dcc#.1dzfvzx4b|date=2016-09-06}}</ref> Brown decided that the world's largest [[Environmental issue|environmental problem]],<ref>{{Cite magazine|title=The Triple Whopper Environmental Impact of Global Meat Production|magazine=Time|url=https://science.time.com/2013/12/16/the-triple-whopper-environmental-impact-of-global-meat-production/|date=2013-12-16|last1=Walsh|first1=Bryan}},</ref> and the problem where he could have the most impact, was the use of [[Livestock|animals]] to produce food.<ref name="Holmes"/>  He organized a conference to raise awareness of the problem.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://dels.nas.edu/resources/static-assets/banr/AnimalProductionMaterials/ScopingWorkshopBackground.pdf |title=The Role of Animal Agriculture in a Sustainable 21st Century Global Food System: A Scoping Workshop |access-date=2016-10-14 |archive-date=2016-10-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161021094856/http://dels.nas.edu/resources/static-assets/banr/AnimalProductionMaterials/ScopingWorkshopBackground.pdf }}</ref> But the National Research Council workshop, called "The Role of Animal Agriculture in a Sustainable 21st Century Global Food System," had minimal impact; soon after, he decided the best way to reduce animal agriculture was to offer a competing product in the free market.<ref name="psmag.com"/>

By the end of his sabbatical, Brown had articulated the first steps of his business plan and began to recruit a small team of scientists to determine precisely why [[meat]] smells, handles, cooks and tastes like meat.<ref name="psmag.com"/> Brown said he had a "hunch" that the key to meat's unique taste was its high abundance of [[heme]], an iron-containing molecule in blood that carries oxygen and is found in all living organisms.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Silicon Valley's Bloody Plant Burger Smells, Tastes And Sizzles Like Meat|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/thesalt/2016/06/21/482322571/silicon-valley-s-bloody-plant-burger-smells-tastes-and-sizzles-like-meat|journal=NPR|date=2016-06-21}}</ref> Brown theorized that, if he could generate large amounts of heme from plant sources, he could recreate the taste of animal meat.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=We tried the plant-based 'impossible burger' that's backed by Bill Gates|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2016/07/29/impossible-burger-our-test-tube-meat-tastes-great.html|journal=CNBC|date=2016-08-02}}</ref>

Brown and a small group of early employees tested the hunch by digging up [[clover]] roots, which for the plant kingdom contain high amounts of heme. "I dissected them off with a razor blade then blended them up just to see what I could extract. I was just poking around, feasibility-testing some ideas. I got to a point where, though I didn't have much data, I had enough to go and talk to some [[venture-capital]] companies — of which there are a ridiculous number in [[Silicon Valley]] — and hit them for some money," Brown told The ''[[Sunday Times]]''.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Can the meat-free Impossible Burger save the world|url=https://www.driving.co.uk/news/lifestyle/impossible-burger/|journal=Sunday Times|date=2017-04-19}}</ref> Brown raised $9 million and founded [[Impossible Foods]] in July 2011.<ref>{{cite news |last=Crews |first=Joel |title=An inside look at Impossible Foods |url=https://www.foodbusinessnews.net/articles/11646-an-inside-look-at-impossible-foods |publisher=Food Business News |date=23 April 2018}}</ref> Over eight years until 2019, the business had collected $396 million from investors like [[Bill Gates]], [[Google Ventures]] and [[Li Ka-shing]]'s [[Horizons Ventures]].<ref name="kgcnbc">{{cite news |last1=Gilchrist |first1=Karen |title=How Impossible Burger's 'simple' vision won hundreds of millions in funding — and backing from Bill Gates |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2019/03/08/bill-gates-backed-impossible-burger-ceo-patrick-brown-on-fighting-meat.html |publisher=CNBC LLC |date=7 March 2019}}</ref>

Brown and his team then spent five years researching and developing the Impossible [[hamburger|Burger]], which launched in restaurants in 2016.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=David Chang Adds Plant Based 'Impossible Burger' to Nishi Menu|url=https://ny.eater.com/2016/7/26/12277310/david-chang-impossible-burger-nishi|journal=Eater|date=2016-07-26}}</ref> Impossible Foods is also working on [[plant]]-based [[pork]], [[chicken]], [[fish]] and [[dairy]] products made without any animals.<ref name="Impossible Foods profile">{{cite news|title=The Secret of These New Veggie Burgers: Plant Blood|newspaper=Wall Street Journal|date=7 October 2014|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/the-secret-of-these-new-veggie-burgers-plant-blood-1412725267|publisher=WSJ|access-date=21 Apr 2015|last1=Rusli|first1=Evelyn M.}}</ref>

The safety of [[soy]] [[leghemoglobin]] produced by [[genetic engineering|genetically engineered]] [[yeast]] was questioned by the [[Food and Drug Administration|FDA]] in 2015.<ref>{{cite news |last=Strom |first=Stephanie |date=2017-08-08 |title=Impossible Burger's 'Secret Sauce' Highlights Challenges of Food Tech |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/08/08/business/impossible-burger-food-meat.html |url-status=live |access-date=2021-12-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231006070521/https://www.nytimes.com/2017/08/08/business/impossible-burger-food-meat.html |archive-date=2023-10-06}}</ref> However, in 2018 the FDA stated that it had "no questions" regarding the safety or regulatory compliance of Impossible Foods' soy leghemoglobin,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.hfpappexternal.fda.gov/scripts/fdcc/index.cfm?set=GRASNotices&id=737 |title=GRN No. 737 Soy leghemoglobin preparation from a strain of Pichia pastoris |date=2018-07-23 |website=GRAS Notice Inventory |publisher=US Food and Drug Administration |access-date=2021-12-08 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author=<!--Staff writer(s)/no by-line.--> |date=2018-07-23 |title=Impossible Foods Receives No-Questions Letter from US Food and Drug Administration |url=https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20180723005786/en/Impossible-Foods-Receives-No-Questions-Letter-from-US-Food-and-Drug-Administration |work=Business Wire |location=Redwood City, CA |access-date=2021-12-08}}</ref> a decision which has since been upheld by the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit|Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Van Voris |first1=Bob |last2=Shanker |first2=Deena |date=2021-05-03 |title=Impossible Foods Wins Ruling to Continue Use of Key Additive |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2021-05-03/impossible-foods-wins-ruling-to-continue-use-of-key-additive |work=Bloomberg |access-date=2021-12-08}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Calma |first=Justine |date=2021-05-03 |title=Impossible Foods clears legal battle over the ingredient that makes its meat 'bleed' |url=https://www.theverge.com/2021/5/3/22418036/impossible-foods-legal-battle-key-ingredient-heme-fda |work=The Verge |access-date=2021-12-08}}</ref>

Brown strongly supports labeling Impossible Foods' products as "meat," regardless of its source. In a 2018 interview with ''[[Quartz (publication)|Quartz]]'', he noted, "animals have just been the technology we have used up until now to produce meat... What consumers value about meat has nothing to do with how it's made. They just live with the fact that it's made from animals. If we're producing a product that is delivering everything that is of value in meat for consumers, it's filling that niche." This assessment, according to Brown, appropriately categorizes meat by "what functional role it plays," rather than its source of origin.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://qz.com/quartzy/1375904/functional-foods-are-boring-someone-tell-silicon-valley/|title=Functional foods are boring. Someone tell Silicon Valley.|last1=Purdy|first1=Chase|website=Quartzy|date=September 2018 |language=en|access-date=2019-05-21}}</ref> These statements have put Brown at odds with the [[meat industry]], which by mid-2019 had successfully pressured state legislatures in [[Missouri]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://qz.com/1372313/a-new-missouri-law-creates-a-definition-of-meat-for-america/|title=A single state wants to determine the definition of meat for America|last1=Purdy|first1=Chase|website=Quartz|date=28 August 2018 |language=en|access-date=2019-05-21}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/2018/08/29/642937901/whats-meat-anyway-missouri-label-law-says-it-comes-from-an-animal-some-disagree|title=What's Meat, Anyway? Missouri Label Law Says It Comes From An Animal; Some Disagree|website=NPR.org|date=29 August 2018 |language=en|access-date=2019-05-21|last1=Sullivan |first1=Emily }}</ref> and [[Arkansas]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://qz.com/1583670/cauliflower-rice-is-a-hot-political-issue-in-arkansas/|title=The war on cauliflower rice|last1=Purdy|first1=Chase|website=Quartz|date=29 March 2019 |language=en|access-date=2019-05-21}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://arktimes.com/arkansas-blog/2019/03/14/legislature-has-a-beef-with-labeling-lab-grown-protein-as-meat|title=Legislature has a beef with labeling lab-grown protein as meat|last=Brantley|first=Max|date=2019-03-14|website=Arkansas Times|language=en-US|access-date=2019-05-21}}</ref> to pass laws barring plant-based protein manufacturers such as Impossible Foods and competitor [[Beyond Meat]] from labeling their products as "meat."

The [[United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change]] strongly endorses Brown's venture and vision, saying that animal-based meat is a "problem" and that in order to "achieve the [[United Nations Sustainable Development Goals]], the global food system must undergo transformative change... By replacing animal products, consumers have enormous power to spare land for biodiversity and carbon capture, halt greenhouse gas emissions at the source, and alleviate demand on fresh water needed for healthy ecosystems."<ref name="fcccif">{{cite news |title=Impossible Foods: Creating Plant-Based Alternatives to Meat {{!}} Singapore, Hong Kong, USA, Macau |url=https://unfccc.int/climate-action/momentum-for-change/planetary-health/impossible-foods |access-date=3 April 2021 |publisher=United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change Secretariat}}</ref>
Research on meats and no-meat substitutes suggests that no-meat products offer substantial benefits over the production of beef, and to a lesser extent pork and chicken, in terms of greenhouse gas production, water and land use.<ref name="Holmes">{{cite journal |last1=Holmes |first1=Bob |title=How sustainable are fake meats? |journal=Knowable Magazine |date=20 July 2022 |doi=10.1146/knowable-071922-1|doi-access=free |url=https://knowablemagazine.org/article/food-environment/2022/how-sustainable-are-fake-meats |access-date=1 August 2022 |language=en|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Awards==
In 2000, Brown received the National Academy of Sciences Award in Molecular Biology.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/patrick-o-brown-cehyef/ | title=NAS Award in Molecular Biology}}</ref>

In 2002 he received a Takeda award, recognizing his work in "the development of DNA microarrays with pre-synthesized DNA probes and the promotion of the technology by releasing the production methods on the Internet."<ref>{{cite press release
  | title =Takeda Award 2002 Achievements Fact Sheet
  | publisher =Takeda Foundation
  | url =http://www.takeda-foundation.jp/en/award/takeda/2002/fact/pdf/fact02.pdf
  | access-date =2007-10-17  }}</ref>

In 2005 he received the [[Curt Stern Award]] for his contributions to the development and application of gene-based expression microarrays.<ref name="curtsternaward">{{Cite journal | last1 = Eichler | first1 = Evan| author-link = Evan Eichler | title = Introductory Speech for Patrick O. Brown* * Previously presented at the annual meeting of the American Society of Human Genetics, in Salt Lake City, on October 29, 2005 | doi = 10.1086/500330 | journal = The American Journal of Human Genetics | volume = 79 | issue = 3 | pages = 427–428 | year = 2006 | pmid = 16909379 | pmc =1559547 }}</ref>

In 2006 he received the [[American Cancer Society]]'s Medal of Honor for Basic Research, acknowledging "his revolutionary development of low-cost, accessible automated microarrays, and his life-saving contributions to the field of functional genomics...which in turn has produced insights into critical genetic information for diseases such as leukemia, lymphoma, prostate cancer, and early stage breast cancer."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://pressroom.cancer.org/2006-11-17-American-Cancer-Society-to-Present-Highest-Honor-to-Katie-Couric-Alice-T-and-William-H-Goodwin-Jr-Mary-Claire-King-and-Patrick-O-Brown-for-Outstanding-Contributions-to-Cancer-Fight | title=American Cancer Society to Present Highest Honor to Katie Couric, Alice T. And William H. Goodwin Jr., Mary-Claire King and Patrick O. Brown for Outstanding Contributions to Cancer Fight}}</ref>

In 2010 the [[Association of Biomolecular Resource Facilities]] (ABRF) selected Brown for the ABRF 2010 Award in recognition of Brown's pioneering work in the development of microarrays and the diverse applications of this technology in genetic research.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://web.cvent.com/event/8eb4a085-b3c5-464a-ba49-023f033a7ee4/summary/archives/abrf2010/index.cfm/page/ConfProg/ABRF_Award.htm/|title=ABRF 2021 Annual Meeting|website=web.cvent.com}}</ref> That year, he also was awarded the Award for Excellence in Molecular Diagnostics by the [[Association for Molecular Pathology]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Past Recipients |url=https://www.amp.org/membership/awards-grants-honors/amp-award-for-excellence-in-molecular-diagnostics/past-recipients/ |access-date=2023-04-12 |website=Association for Molecular Pathology |language=en}}</ref>

In 2016, [[Klaus Schwab]] and the [[World Economic Forum]] named Brown and his company a "Technology Pioneer" for their design, development and deployment of new technologies and innovations "poised to have a significant impact on business and society."<ref name=wefvid>[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8Pya2sW7my0 Technology Pioneer 2016 - Patrick O Brown (Impossible Foods)] (World Economic Forum)</ref> Their citation reads: "Impossible Foods is creating meat and dairy substitutes directly from plants. They aim to eliminate the destructive environmental impact of the global animal farming industry by inventing sustainable and scalable ways to produce delicious, nutritious and affordable meat and dairy foods. Their technology transforms nutrients from plant crops directly into foods that have the flavours and textures of meat and dairy products, with all of the nutritional value."<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://widgets.weforum.org/techpioneers-2016/|title=Technology Pioneers 2016 - World Economic Forum|website=widgets.weforum.org}}</ref>

In 2018, the [[United Nations Environment Programme]] named [[Impossible Foods]] and [[Beyond Meat]] joint winners of the Champions of the Earth Award, in the Science and Innovation category. Pat Brown and [[Ethan Brown (businessman)|Ethan Brown]] (the CEO of Beyond Meat, who is unrelated) were awarded the award for production of sustainable alternatives to beef meats.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Champions of the Earth | url=https://www.unep.org/championsofearth/node/48 |access-date=2023-10-24 |website=UNEP |language=en}}</ref>
